questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The University of California, Los Angeles is world renowned for its world-class mathematics department. I was drawn to the prospect of receiving education from some of the greatest mathematicians in the world.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Los Angeles is an expensive city to reside in, and our exchange agreement with UCLA is strictly for a six-month stay. Staying 6 months in a city where rent is typically $1500 a month was difficult for me financially. However, overall, I had a great experience abroad.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I received most needed information through the host university’s email system. However, I missed a few events at the very beginning of my stay, as my UCEAP Reciprocity account did not link with my UCLA email at first. Instead, a lot of relevant mail got sent to my UCPH mail, which I did think to check regularly at the time. Luckily, this was quite easy to correct manually.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I needed assistance from the UCPH study guidance to confirm my arrival, as Mobility Online was broken at the time. I also received mandatory vaccinations from the Arthur Ashe Student Health and Wellness Center a few days after my arrival.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The "iSTART orientation" and "SHAPE training" at UCLA felt like a huge waste of time. Moreover, it would have been nice to know that the mandatory vaccinations at UCLA were all covered by my (mandatory) US health insurance. I ended up paying 1100 kr. for vaccinations in Denmark that I could have gotten for free in the US.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was relatively easy. I found a host on Airbnb, who hosted me through Airbnb for one month. After that, when she got to know my situation, she offered to host me permanently at a discounted rate.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
That public transport in LA is surprisingly good. The buses to UCLA are frequent and on time. Moreover, the city’s metro network is currently being expanded to Westwood. I imagine that the metro line next to UCLA will be open in a year or two for future exchange students to use.

Biking in LA is also surprisingly doable (despite what you will hear some people say). There are bike lanes all over Santa Monica, and most of West LA is generally quite bikeable as well.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: On campus housing is not meant for exchange students. Most housing contracts are for one year minimum with heavy fines if you leave early.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: We were forced to complete the "iSTART orientation" program. It was alright, but a lot of it felt redundant and mundane. I felt like time would have been better spent with study-focused mixer events, like the voluntary ones offered by the Dashew Center.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Dashew Center for International Students & Scholars is an on-campus building/institution designed for helping and guiding exchange students. They were incredibly helpful throughout (for instance, when I needed a TIN-number for my Danish bank), and I am thankful they were around.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful. I was told that I would probably not be able to enroll in more than two graduate courses for the duration of my stay. This was luckily not the case, as the mathematics department let me enroll in more or less all the courses I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: For anyone going on exchange to a UC campus during their master’s studies (like myself), my advice would be that one can typically enroll in as many graduate courses as they’d like, despite what UC might tell you at first. This can be an unnecessary deal-breaker for some, and I think it is unfortunate that the communication is not more clear.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was quite happy with all the courses I took. The only exception was my participation in the course “Math 246B - Complex Analysis”. I did not take the prerequisite course “Math 246A - Complex Analysis”, which the lecturer ensured me was not important. This was a lie. I struggled a lot with the course, and I ended up spending way more time than I should have just to pass. This course completely ruined my GPA, which I think is a little unfortunate, as I simply did not have the proper prerequisites for participating. Better communication from the lecturer would have been appreciated.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took the following undergraduate courses (BA level): “Math 135 - Ordinary Differential Equations” and “Math 155 - Mathematical Imaging”. In addition, I took the following graduate courses (MA level): “Math 273A - Optimization and Calculus of Variations: Basic Optimization Theory”, “Math 246B - Complex Analysis”, “Math 247A - Classical Fourier Analysis” and “Math 254B - Topics in Real Analysis”.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was mostly the same. Due to the federal funding cuts happening in the US at the time of my exchange program, there were no exercise classes in any of my courses. This felt a bit hollow, as I have had exercise classes at UCPH in all the courses I have taken thus far. Other than that, the courses at UCLA felt quite similar in structure to what I am used to.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: In my first semester (that is, in my first quarter), I was enrolled in the following courses: “Math 135 - Ordinary Differential Equations”, “Math 155 - Mathematical Imaging” and “Math 273A - Optimization and Calculus of Variations: Basic Optimization Theory”.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
questions.answer: In my second semester (that is, in my second quarter), I was enrolled in the following courses: “Math 246B - Complex Analysis”, “Math 247A - Classical Fourier Analysis” and “Math 254B - Topics in Real Analysis”.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: It is difficult for me to say, as I did not experience the courses in full due to the lack of exercise classes. However, I quite enjoyed “Math 155 - Mathematical Imaging”. As a pure mathematician, it was a nice (and rigorous) introduction to an interesting area of applied mathematics. Moreover, I also quite enjoyed “Math 247A - Classical Fourier Analysis”, but this course is probably more tailored to a dedicated pure math crowd.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: There were quite a few unexpected expenses at the onset of the exchange program. There were fees associated with obtaining a US visa, like the SEVIS fee, the booking fee at the embassy and the price of being photographed by a licensed photographer. In addition, there were some mandatory fees that needed to be paid to UCLA before they would allow me to enroll in their courses. I am still not entirely sure what these fees were, but I was forced to pay them via the university’s billing service “BruinBill”. In general, I was quite surprised by the number of unexpected expenses that kept appearing in the beginning. Luckily, this evened out a bit toward the end of my stay.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I had no expenses for textbooks and school supplies whatsoever. All of the courses I took either used freely accessible textbooks or free notes as class material. Conversely, I was a bit surprised about the high cost of living in LA. I was prepared to pay a higher rent than usual, but I did not expect the price of groceries to be about 20% higher than at home.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: By the nature of sports and athletics at US universities, it was not possible for me to participate in any sporting activity associated with UCLA, as these programs are strictly reserved for “student athletes” (meaning athletes who pretend to be students in order to play for the university’s sports teams). This was a bit disappointing to me, but I understand that it is a biproduct of a cultural convention. Luckily, there were many other social events organized by the university that I enjoyed attending. Specifically, I really liked the “Bruin Mixer” events organized by the Dashew Center. These events gave me a chance to meet other exchange students, who were also new in town, and were the basis of some of the best friendships I made throughout my stay.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Personally, I did not do a lot of non-academic activities during my stay. I went to the beach once, which I would recommend. Moreover, I went out partying a few times in Westwood, Venice Beach and West Hollywood, which were all good experiences. However, by personal choice/preference, I spent a lot of time studying throughout my stay and I did not do much off-campus activity.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Beside visiting the well-known tourist destinations around LA, I would very much encourage future exchange students to attend a few university sports games. The spectacle surrounding university sports in the US makes this quite intriguing (and typically also quite cheap if you are a student). In addition, I also found it quite entertaining to watch non-university sports games in the downtown area. Personally, I watched the LA Kings play in the NHL twice during my stay, but I also heard good things from friends who watched the LA Lakers and LA Rams play on other occasions.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Incredibly easy. Despite what you will hear in a lot of media nowadays, it is my honest impression that Americans are an overwhelmingly friendly, open and welcoming people. LA in particular seems to be a very inclusive place, and I had no trouble coexisting with the many people I met throughout.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I would strongly encourage all exchange students at UCLA to participate in the “Bruin Mixer” events. These helped me immensely with socializing and finding friends when I first arrived.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It is hard to pin down exactly, but many things at UCLA (and in the US in general) insisted on encouraging a type of behavior that I would best describe as “play to the gallery”. For instance, many of the courses I took at UCLA had a system of “extra credit”, where one could obtain a better grade for a course by doing something mundane like attending a one-hour seminar. This seemed quite odd to me, as I ended up having a feeling that certain course grades were not representative of one’s academic performance, but instead a measure of how well one was at jumping though some arbitrary hoops that the lecturer had come up with. In my experience, this sentiment was echoed throughout many aspects of American culture, which I found quite different from what I was used to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The hospitality and openness of the American people. The people I met were typically very accepting and inclusive and seemed to have little to no bias towards my cultural background. I found this inspiring.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
My list of the three most important things to know before embarking on an exchange program at UCLA would probably rank as follows:

1) Save up a lot of money. Apply for as many scholarships as possible and save all the money you can whenever you can (i.e., by buying the cheapest possible plane tickets). LA is an expensive city, and you will have to make a living there for 6 months without a student job.

2) It is very common for both native UCLA students and exchange students to leave town for Christmas. If you are therefore staying for both fall and winter quarter, you should not plan on celebrating Christmas with fellow UCLA students.

3) The time zone difference of nine hours to Denmark makes communication with friends and family difficult. If you have important matters to tend to with people back home, do so before departing for LA.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would encourage all future exchange students at UCLA to make diligent preparations for housing in LA. Specifically, I would recommend people to make living arrangements with other exchange students from UCPH ahead of time. Having a roommate from UCPH would have helped me immensely throughout my stay, but, sadly, I had none. Worse yet, I later met other exchange students from UCPH in LA, who told me they were in the same predicament and that they would have been happy to share a room with me.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I was (strongly) encouraged by a UCLA professor to apply for a PhD position at a university that she will be moving to shortly. The professor in question is a renowned mathematics professor, and obtaining this kind of acknowledgement from her means the world to me. I will be applying for the PhD position this fall. If anything comes of it, it will, in and of itself, be worth every penny and hour I spend throughout my stay.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The nine-hour time difference between LA and Denmark was at times difficult for me to deal with. I was never homesick, nor did I feel a strong need to stay in constant contact with people back home. However, it became increasingly frustrating that I could not reach family and friends about practical matters at normal times of the day. This was especially noticeable toward the end of my stay, when I had to sign up for courses and TA positions at UCPH and make plans for the Easter holidays with friends and family - all while the people I needed to contact were asleep.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: As mentioned earlier, I regret not having found a roommate from UCPH before departing for LA. I think this could, in part, have been helped by UCPH, if they had provided us with a list of other students, who were embarking on the same exchange agreement as us. It might be against certain GDPR laws to do so without permission, but from what I have heard, everyone from UCPH would happily have given permission for such a list to be sent out. Many exchange students from other universities received a list like this, and they were all very happy about it. I think it is a shame that we were not provided with one.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
